thread.title: Alphabet Has No Excuses Not To Pay A Dividend - Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG)

author: Julian Lin
title: Alphabet Has No Excuses Not To Pay A Dividend - Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG)
text:
Thesis Alphabet ( GOOG ) is a stock which I have not written a focus article yet despite many times writing that it is my largest position. While I do believe that this is the strongest business model on the planet with many years of growth still to come (after all it is my largest position), I do however have the opinion that management’s decision to avoid paying a dividend to be entirely misguided. The old excuse that they need to reinvest all cash no longer rings true in light of a rapidly growing cash hoard. Starting a dividend program, even small, would be a low risk high reward allocation decision that would surely payoff in the years to come.
Business Overview GOOG is an online advertising giant deriving most of its revenues from advertising through its search and YouTube offerings:
( 2017 10-K )
Their advertising division continues to see extremely robust revenue growth in spite of its size. The growth is primarily coming from growth in advertisements sold as they have indeed seen prices fall:
(2017 10-K)
I view the pricing pressures to be very near term as this is a growth story that is still taking off the ground and still has miles left to run.
MOAT If your child has flu-like symptoms, do you call your doctor first, or do you ask Google?
If you wanted to learn how to change your child’s diapers, do you call up your parents or do you watch some YouTube videos?
Such name brand is indicative of the famed “moat” business model which investing legends such as Warren Buffett have raved about. Moat businesses allow for strong revenue growth as they take market share and eventually exert pricing power down the road. GOOG’s firm control of the search and video streaming markets enables it to be the primary beneficiary of the trends towards the internet, e-commerce, and of course online advertising. Yes, their revenues are already very large and yes, their market capitalization is almost enough to swallow a whole country but readers should not underestimate the market size of both online advertising and in general, the internet.
No dividend yet - but they should pay one While GOOG has certainly performed extremely well for the past decade, I suspect many readers may have missed out on the ride because of one important detail: they do not pay regular dividends.
Since many investors exclusively invest in dividend paying stocks, the fact that GOOG chooses not to payout dividends alienates an entire group of prospective investors as it misses out inclusion in many indexes. I argue that GOOG should be paying a dividend and should start doing it now.
Don’t they need to reinvest all cash? The biggest argument I hear to avoid dividend payouts among tech stocks is that they need to reinvest all cash flows. While in theory this is an argument with practical sense, as after all earnings growth should be prioritized over “boring” dividends.
But is this really the case with GOOG? GOOG lists its dividend policy as follows: “We have never declared or paid any cash dividend on our common or capital stock. We intend to retain any future earnings and do not expect to pay any cash dividends in the foreseeable future.” (2017 10-K)
We can see below that their cash hoard has been growing to its most recent sum of $102.9 billion:
(Chart by author, data from 10-K)
These cash and marketable securities balance in general are being held with maturities of 1-5 years:
(2017 10-K)
With interest rates at historic lows, this implies very low yields. The growing cash hoard plus low reinvestment yields leads me to conclude definitively that they no longer should be retaining all cash flow.
Even something small will count I am not proposing that they start paying a large dividend (although that would be nice). But surely they can afford a $1/ share payout? With 705 million shares outstanding, this would come to a total payout of around $705 million. Considering that their cash hoard continues to grow by much faster than this amount, I do not buy any argument that they can not afford this payout.
Why the dividend matters I believe that they should institute this payout policy immediately with the aim of intending to increase it every year, even if the increase is only by 10 cents annually. Such an increase would, due to the low starting payout amount, already be a 10% growth rate. Having a dividend growth history is extremely important. Every year that they do not pay a dividend is one less potential year for their dividend growth history. Many investors screen for stocks paying consistently growing dividends, in fact there are exclusive indexes containing such stocks such as those known as dividend aristocrats, dividend achievers, and dividend kings.
While some may be thinking that such a payout is too small to be significant, please entertain me for a little longer. Even the most bullish investors must agree that at some point GOOG will be unable to sustain a measurable amount of growth. This may happen in the event of new competitors, an economic slowdown, or in general simply companies maximizing their advertising budgets. At this point, the stock price is likely to experience extreme volatility, especially if the earnings slowdown is announced during earnings when the multiple trades around 20-25 times. Growth investors would be forced to sell shares as it would no longer fit their fund rules.
Let’s consider what would happen instead if GOOG has been paying a growing dividend and let’s assume that this event is ten years in the future. I believe that the volatility would be much better managed as there would be a large pool of buyers ready to play the other side of the forced selling. It would not be so crazy to imagine a dividend growth stock with a streak of ten years trading at 20 times earnings - the same however can not be said for a non-dividend stock with no growth. For a recent example, we can examine the history of none other than Apple ( AAPL ):
( Yahoo Finance )
We can see that AAPL dropped significantly in 2015-2016 when it became clear that the secular growth age of iPhones was coming to an end. Their dividend payouts starting in 2012 due to the advice of Carl Icahn may have helped ease the fall, but I do believe that if the dividends were begun much earlier that the volatility experienced here would have been much more contained.
In summary, starting a dividend growth history now would have no risk (since they certainly can afford a small payout) and high reward (in helping to manage volatility down the road).
Other benefits of a dividend With such a cash hoard building up, it is only natural for shareholders to wonder what other uses does management really have in mind with the cash. The recently renewed $8.6 billion share repurchase authorization won’t make a dent in their cash hoard. Perhaps they may be considering making several large acquisitions? With equities all in general trading richly valued, would such an acquisition really be the best use of capital? Paying a dividend would help eliminate these fears as a dividend shows clearly management’s commitment to generate shareholder value.
Balance Sheet With $4 billion in debt on the balance sheet versus $102.9 billion in cash and marketable securities, it is clear that Alphabet has not been tapping the debt markets as aggressively as peers. Readers should see this as a clear positive as in future years they may use this as a catalyst to unlock shareholder value by levering up the balance sheet to support share repurchases.
Valuation Trading at just 20 times forward earnings, GOOG remains extremely discounted in light of their ultra-high quality earnings growth. This is the kind of stock which I believe would demand a 20 times multiple even when earnings growth slows down to a crawl due to their continued knack for innovation. As such, it does not make sense to trade at their terminal multiple when they still have strong earnings growth predicted for the next decade. A more suitable multiple would be 30 times forward earnings or about $1500 per share. I would not even be surprised if GOOG trades at 40 times forward earnings or about $2000 per share. To say I am most optimistically bullish on GOOG is an understatement.
Think beyond search Many have counted GOOG out as a “one trick pony” due to their reliance on search and YouTube. I won’t be the first to point out that they have been investing heavily in other markets such as cloud, Waymo (self-driving cars), and smartphones (Google Pixel). However I need to emphasize that search and YouTube should be seen as platforms upon which they can continue building on and monetizing their large network of users. When you have such a large network of engaged users, it becomes easy to earn a little more through new add-ons. Some examples I could think of are online education (YouTube), online travel bookings (search), and portable automatic translating devices (Google translate). The sky is the limit when you have the best products.
Conclusion GOOG is in my opinion one of the most attractively priced stocks in the market. It is very rare to be able to buy a company with strong sustained earnings for 20 times earnings. Buy for 40-50% near term upside but hold this one forever.
